# WDT Q&A

Imagine owning a tree as an investment. If it grows, you share a small portion of that year's growth through tax. If a storm damages it and its value falls, the government shares part of the loss. That is the basic idea behind the Wealth Delta Tax (WDT). Instead of taxing what people earn, spend, or choose to sell, it taxes only the annual change in a person's net worth. The government becomes a passive partner: it shares in gains, shares in losses, and because the economy's wealth tends to grow over time, it receives a positive return overall.

The money is first paid into a Sovereign Wealth Fund, which builds the reserves needed to fund refunds during downturns. As the economy grows, the fund accumulates assets. Once it reaches its target size, future net revenue is used to reduce taxes on labour, allowing people to keep more of what they earn. The result is a tax system that shares both risk and reward while gradually shifting part of the tax burden from work to increases in accumulated wealth.


| Objection                                                                 | WDT Answer                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Addressed in                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **1. "If gains and losses are symmetrical, won't it raise no money?"**    | No. Symmetry means individuals are treated fairly, not that aggregate revenue is zero. The government becomes a passive partner in the economy, sharing a fixed proportion of gains and losses. Because total private wealth is expected to grow over time, gains exceed losses over the long run, producing positive expected revenue. The Sovereign Wealth Fund smooths the inevitable year-to-year volatility.                                                     | **WP** (mechanism overview); **RATES** (revenue modelling and long-run revenue capacity); **RATES.A** (simulation models); **MF** (reciprocal partnership principle); **ENV** (economic transmission channels)                                                   |
| **2. "How can the government afford refunds in a crash?"**                | Refunds are pre-funded. All WDT revenue first capitalises the Sovereign Wealth Fund Refund Reserve (SRR) before being used for other purposes. The SWF exists specifically because a symmetric system creates a genuine liability during downturns. The government does not promise refunds without first building the capacity to honour them.                                                                                                                       | **WP** (SWF role); **RATES** (SRR capitalisation and solvency modelling); **RATES.A** (SWF Solvency Model); **GOV** (Custodian mandate and solvency floor); **GOV.B** (operational SWF specification)                                                            |
| **3. "Annual valuation is impossible."**                                  | The WDT does not require the government to know the perfect value of every asset. It creates incentives so that honest declaration becomes the rational strategy. Different asset classes use different valuation routes. Because a declared value becomes the future tax basis, systematic understatement delays rather than eliminates tax and creates future exposure.                                                                                             | **VAL** (valuation architecture); **VAL.A** (mathematical validation and incentive simulations); **VAL.B** (worked examples); **BEHAV** (behavioural robustness); **GOV** (Valuation Body governance)                                                            |
| **4. "Won't people just hide or move their wealth?"**                     | Traditional avoidance strategies are weakened because the tax applies to changes in net worth rather than transactions. Hiding wealth creates future basis problems and forfeits protection under the refund system. Corporate ownership gaps are addressed through the corporate instrument. Exit is treated as a legitimate closure event rather than something requiring punitive taxation. Remaining behavioural responses are empirical questions for Phase One. | **BEHAV** (avoidance taxonomy, enforcement paradigm, migration analysis); **VAL** (self-correction and declaration incentives); **CORP** (corporate attribution gap); **CLOSE** (exit framework); **PHASE1** (empirical questions requiring implementation data) |
| **5. "Isn't this just another wealth tax?"**                              | No. Traditional wealth taxes tax the stock of wealth simply because it exists. The WDT taxes only the annual change in wealth. If wealth does not increase, no tax is owed. If wealth falls, a refund is paid. The mechanism is therefore closer to a partnership in investment outcomes than a charge on ownership.                                                                                                                                                  | **WP** (core mechanism); **MF** (wealth as present economic power); **LR.B** (wealth tax literature comparison); **RATES** (delta-based revenue model)                                                                                                           |
| **6. "Will people have to sell assets just to pay the tax?"**             | The design avoids unnecessary forced realisation. Different asset routes provide different settlement methods: professional valuation routes, deferred settlement, liens, in-kind settlement where appropriate, and realisation-based treatment for assets where interim settlement would be inappropriate. Liquidity constraints are treated as a design requirement.                                                                                                | **VAL** (asset routes and settlement architecture); **VAL.A** (mechanical validation); **CLOSE** (settlement at closure events); **CORP** (listed-company treatment)                                                                                             |
| **7. "Why tax unrealised gains?"**                                        | Because wealth creates economic advantages even before an asset is sold. Existing systems allow people to defer taxation indefinitely by avoiding realisation, encouraging lock-in and borrowing against assets. The WDT taxes the increase in economic capacity as it occurs while providing downside protection through refunds.                                                                                                                                    | **WP** (tax base rationale); **MF** (wealth as present power, not deferred consumption); **ENV** (lock-in and efficiency analysis); **LR.B** (intellectual background)                                                                                           |
| **8. "Why should government invest alongside private wealth?"**           | The WDT reframes the state-taxpayer relationship as reciprocal. The state already benefits when wealth grows but historically does not share downside risk. By accepting losses as well as gains, government creates a symmetrical relationship that supports legitimacy and risk-sharing.                                                                                                                                                                            | **MF** (reciprocity as foundational axiom); **WP** (cooperative architecture); **GOV** (institutional expression of reciprocity); **LR.B** (Domar-Musgrave and risk-sharing background)                                                                          |
| **9. "What if the economy stops growing?"**                               | WDT revenue would fall during prolonged weak growth, just as other tax revenues fall during economic downturns. The system does not assume every year is positive; it is designed around long-term averages. The SWF exists to absorb temporary periods when refunds exceed revenue.                                                                                                                                                                                  | **RATES** (historical sensitivity testing); **RATES.A** (73-start-year simulations and stress testing); **ENV** (macroeconomic transmission); **GOV.B** (SWF resilience mechanisms)                                                                              |
| **10. "Why have a Sovereign Wealth Fund instead of spending the money?"** | Because the refund obligation is not optional—it is a core part of the WDT promise. The SWF separates refund security from government spending decisions. Only after the refund reserve and required capitalisation targets are met can revenue flow toward labour tax relief.                                                                                                                                                                                        | **WP** (SWF purpose); **RATES** (SRR/LRR structure); **GOV** (constitutional constraints); **GOV.B** (operational mandate)                                                                                                                                       |
| **11. "Why use the money to cut labour taxes?"**                          | Reducing taxes on labour is the stated purpose of the mature WDT system. The goal is not simply to raise revenue, but to shift part of the tax burden away from work and toward increases in accumulated wealth. A system that taxed wealth deltas but left labour taxation unchanged would not achieve the project's objective.                                                                                                                                      | **WP** (labour relief dividend); **RATES** (LRR and transition model); **GOV** (enumerated clause committing revenue use); **ENV** (labour and consumption transmission channels)                                                                                |
| **12. "Does everyone have to pay this?"**                                 | No. The WDT uses a high exemption threshold so the substantial majority of households are excluded. Phase One begins with an even higher threshold affecting a small population, allowing infrastructure, valuation systems, and behavioural evidence to develop before scaling.                                                                                                                                                                                      | **WP** (scope and exemption); **MF** (capacity-to-bear rationale); **RATES** (threshold modelling); **PHASE1** (implementation pathway)                                                                                                                          |
